title: Question Surface — how it ships
intro:
Decisions that gate turning this from a folder inside one repo into a tool any agent can install and call. Everything here is open; nothing is being re-asked.

Already settled and not on this form: it stays stdlib-only, loopback-only, and browser-launched with no interface of its own; it gets semver, tags, and a changelog; `serve` stays a blocking call that self-terminates on submit.

Anything you don't know yet, tick **Don't know** — that flags it as research rather than a blank, and it becomes a work item instead of a question I ask you again.

sections.title: Shape of the install
sections.intro: How a fresh machine — or a fresh Claude instance in an unrelated project — gets this.

questions.prompt: Today the tool only works from inside its own directory: `QUESTIONNAIRES` and `RESPONSES` resolve relative to `qsurface.py`, and the skill is found only because it sits in that repo's `.claude/skills/`. Both have to change for a global install, and they change independently — that is the first two sections.
What is the primary install route?
questions.why: This decides what I build and what the README's first code block says. It also decides who can use the tool: a Claude Code plugin reaches Claude Code and nothing else, while a CLI on `PATH` reaches anything that can run a shell command — which is your stated goal of *any* LLM being able to call it.

options.label: `git clone` + `./install.sh`
options.detail: The installer symlinks the skill into `~/.claude/skills/` and puts `qsurface` on `PATH`. Same pattern you already run for the access ledger, so it is one house style rather than two. Works for any agent runtime, not just Claude Code.

options.label: Claude Code plugin from a marketplace repo
options.detail: `/plugin install` and the skill arrives with it. Lowest friction inside Claude Code. Cost: it is Claude-Code-only, so an LLM outside Claude Code gets nothing, and the Python CLI still needs a home.

options.label: Both — `install.sh` as the real installer, plus a thin plugin manifest
options.detail: Covers Claude Code users and everyone else. Cost: two install paths to keep working and to test on every release.

options.label: `uv tool install git+https://…`
options.detail: Familiar to Python users and handles `PATH` for you. Cost: adds `uv` as an install-time dependency, and it does not place the skill — that stays a manual step, which is the part most likely to be skipped.

questions.prompt: Should the installer symlink the skill into `~/.claude/skills/`, or copy it?
questions.why: A symlink means `git pull` in the clone updates the skill everywhere immediately, including breaking changes you did not ask for right then. A copy means the skill is stable until you re-run the installer, and can silently go stale against a newer CLI.

options.label: Symlink
options.detail: One source of truth. The skill and the CLI can never disagree about which version they are.

options.label: Copy, refreshed by re-running the installer
options.detail: Predictable — nothing changes under you mid-session. Cost: a stale skill describing flags the installed CLI doesn't have.

questions.prompt: Public or private repository?
questions.why: Public allows a one-line install from a raw URL and makes the README the documentation. Private means every install needs an authenticated clone, which is a real friction cost on a new machine.

options.label: Public
options.detail: Nothing in the tool is proprietary — the extraction already removed everything that was. Simplest install story.

options.label: Private
options.detail: Install requires auth. Fine if you would rather not maintain something people file issues against.

questions.prompt: Repository name
questions.why: Also becomes the clone directory and, if it goes on `PATH` under its own name, part of what you type. The CLI itself is `qsurface` either way.

questions.prompt: Who creates and pushes the GitHub repo?
questions.why: Creating a repo under your account and pushing to it is an outward-facing action I will not take on assumption. Tell me which half is mine.

options.label: I create it with `gh` and push, then hand you the URL
options.detail: Fastest. I will confirm the exact name and visibility with you before the create call runs.

options.label: You create the empty repo; I add the remote and push
options.detail: You keep control of naming, org, and settings; I do the mechanical part.

options.label: Stay local for now
options.detail: Keeps tagging and changelog discipline without publishing yet. Install story becomes 'clone from a path'.

sections.title: Where questionnaires and responses live
sections.intro: Once the tool is global, its data cannot live next to the code that runs it.

questions.prompt: This is the decision with the longest tail. Responses are records of decisions, and where they land determines whether they are findable a year from now by the person reading the project — or only by someone who knows the tool exists.
Where do questionnaires and responses go?
questions.why: Everything downstream depends on this: whether responses can be code-reviewed alongside the change they justify, whether two projects can collide, and whether a response survives someone uninstalling the tool.

options.label: In the project being worked on
options.detail: A decision lands in the repo it is about and can be committed in the same PR as the work it gates. Cost: adds a directory to every project that uses it.

options.label: In the tool's install directory (today's behaviour)
options.detail: Nothing is added to your projects. Cost: every project's answers pile up in one unrelated folder, detached from the work, and are lost if the clone is deleted.

options.label: A central state directory keyed by project
options.detail: Projects stay clean and nothing collides. Cost: the decision record is no longer in the repo, so it is invisible to code review and to anyone who clones the project.

options.label: Configurable, defaulting to the project
options.detail: An env var or config file overrides it. Cost: a config surface to document and support, and two behaviours to test.

questions.prompt: What is that directory called inside a project?
questions.why: It shows up in every repo that uses the tool. A dotted name stays out of the way; a plain name is more discoverable to a human who was not told it exists.

options.label: `.question-surface/`
options.detail: Hidden, unambiguous, sorts out of the way. Matches the convention of tool-owned directories.

options.label: `questions/`
options.detail: Visible and obvious to a human browsing the repo. Cost: a fairly generic name to claim at the top level.

options.label: `docs/decisions/`
options.detail: Files responses as project documentation rather than tool output. Cost: mixes generated records with hand-written docs.

questions.prompt: Should responses be committed to the host project's git by default?
questions.why: This is the durability argument the whole tool rests on. If responses are ignored by default, the answers end up exactly where the chat transcript was — somewhere nobody re-reads.

options.label: Tracked — the installer writes no ignore rule
options.detail: Responses are reviewable and survive. Cost: answers you gave casually are in the repo history.

options.label: Ignored by default
options.detail: Nothing lands in the project history unless someone opts in. Cost: the durability claim goes away.

options.label: Neither — the skill tells the agent to ask
options.detail: No default imposed. Cost: it will be inconsistent across projects.

questions.prompt: Should `qsurface` stage the response file itself after a submit?
questions.why: Convenient, but it means a tool you ran to ask a question has touched your git index — which is surprising if you were mid-commit on something unrelated.

options.label: No — the tool never touches git
options.detail: The agent commits it as part of the task, which is where the decision belongs anyway.

options.label: Yes — `git add` the response on submit
options.detail: One less step to forget. Cost: mutates the index of a repo the tool does not own.

sections.title: The loop an agent drives
sections.intro: You described: build surface → serve → present link → wait → parse → terminate. That already works. These are the edges around it.

questions.prompt: Confirmed from the code: `serve` blocks until submit, then stops the accept loop and returns, and the process exits — so the server does terminate on its own. It now also releases the socket rather than holding the port. **What it does not have is a way to stop waiting.** If nobody ever submits, it waits forever.
Keep `serve` blocking, or add a non-blocking start/stop pair?
questions.why: Blocking matches the loop you described and needs no state files. A start/stop pair lets an agent keep working while you answer, at the cost of a pid file, a status command, and orphaned-server cleanup.

options.label: Blocking only
options.detail: The agent backgrounds the call and gets woken when it exits. No new state to manage, no orphan servers. This is what runs today.

options.label: Add `start` / `status` / `stop`
options.detail: The agent can poll and do other work meanwhile. Cost: pid/state files, stale-state handling, and a way to kill a server whose agent went away.

options.label: Both
options.detail: Blocking stays the documented path; the trio is there when needed. Cost: two lifecycles to test and document.

questions.prompt: Should waiting time out?
questions.why: Without a timeout, a questionnaire you walk away from leaves a Python process and a bound port alive indefinitely, and the agent's background job never returns. With one, an unanswered form has a defined end.

options.label: `--timeout`, with a default
options.detail: Sensible default, overridable for a long questionnaire you want to leave open. I would set the default around two hours.

options.label: A fixed timeout, not configurable
options.detail: One less flag. Cost: the wrong number is the wrong number everywhere.

options.label: No timeout — wait forever
options.detail: Simplest. Cost: the failure mode above, which an agent cannot detect or recover from.

questions.prompt: What happens when it times out?
questions.why: This decides what the calling agent believes. A non-zero exit reads as 'no answers yet, still blocked'; a written response reads as 'this is what we got', which is wrong if you were simply away from the desk.

options.label: Save the draft, exit non-zero, write nothing
options.detail: The agent reports it is still waiting and can re-serve later — the draft means nothing typed is lost.

options.label: Write a response marked incomplete
options.detail: The agent gets whatever was filled in and can proceed on partial information. Cost: a partial record that looks like a decision.

questions.prompt: What is the default gate, for someone who never configures one?
questions.why: The gate is the thing that actually changes agent behaviour — the tool existing does not. Five was chosen for a repo where architecture forks were the common case; a general-purpose tool ships to people who will never touch the setting, so the default is what most installs will run.

options.label: Five or more
options.detail: Proven in use. Four or fewer stays in chat, which keeps quick exchanges quick.

options.label: Three or more
options.detail: Catches more batches. Cost: spinning up a browser form for three questions is heavier than the questions deserve.

options.label: No hard floor — the skill describes when it helps
options.detail: More judgement, less mechanism. Cost: a soft rule is one the model talks itself out of, which is how the failure mode returns.

questions.prompt: How does a user change that number for themselves?
questions.why: A skill is static markdown, so the number cannot simply be a setting the skill reads at runtime — the model has to either be told it up front or spend a tool call finding out. That tradeoff is the whole question: a value that is always in context costs a file the tool does not own, and a value that is looked up costs a call the model may skip.

options.label: A config file, plus a one-line pointer the installer adds to your global `CLAUDE.md`
options.detail: `qsurface config set gate 3` is the source of truth; the pointer line puts the current number in context for every session with no tool call. Cost: the installer edits `~/.claude/CLAUDE.md`, which it does not own — it would ask first and be reversible.

options.label: A config file the skill tells the agent to read
options.detail: Nothing outside the tool's own directories is touched. Cost: the agent must run `qsurface gate` to learn the threshold, and the moment it is unsure it will guess the default instead.

options.label: The installer writes the number into the installed skill text
options.detail: Always in context, zero tool calls, nothing else touched. Cost: only works if the skill is a copy rather than a symlink, so it conflicts with the symlink option earlier — and the number goes stale if you edit the config directly.

options.label: An environment variable
options.detail: No files, trivially overridable per project. Cost: it lives in a shell profile the agent cannot see, so in practice the model never knows it changed.

options.label: Not settable — one number for everyone
options.detail: Least machinery, and the rule stays legible. Cost: the number is wrong for anyone whose work is shaped differently than yours.

questions.prompt: Expose the tool over MCP as well as the CLI?
questions.why: An MCP server would let MCP-capable clients call it as a typed tool rather than shelling out. It is the difference between 'any agent with a shell' and 'any agent at all', and it is a meaningful amount of additional surface to maintain.

options.label: Not now — revisit once the CLI is in use
options.detail: The CLI already covers every runtime that can run a command, which is most of them. Keeps v1 small.

options.label: Build it as part of this work
options.detail: Covers clients that cannot shell out. Cost: a second interface to version, and MCP servers are a stdlib-only constraint's least favourite thing.

options.label: No — CLI only, permanently
options.detail: One interface forever.

questions.prompt: Add a `spec_version` field to the questionnaire format?
questions.why: You said questionnaires authored against one format have to keep working against later ones. Without a version field in the document, the loader cannot tell an old spec from a malformed one, so the only safe migration is never changing the format.

options.label: Yes — validated, defaulting to 1 when absent
options.detail: Existing questionnaires keep loading, and a future breaking change has somewhere to branch. Cheap now, impossible to retrofit cleanly later.

options.label: No — keep the format as-is
options.detail: One less field to explain. Cost: the format is effectively frozen, or old questionnaires break silently.

questions.prompt: Add GitHub Actions running the test suite?
questions.why: You asked for no bugs. The suite is 37 tests and runs in under a second; the thing it cannot catch is a change that breaks on a Python version you don't have locally.

options.label: Yes — on push and PR, across supported Python versions
options.detail: Catches the version-drift class of break, which is the realistic one for a stdlib-only tool that must still run in a year.

options.label: Yes — one Python version only
options.detail: Cheaper and faster. Cost: blind to the exact failure CI is most useful for here.

options.label: No CI
options.detail: Tests run when someone remembers to run them.

questions.prompt: Should the client-side JavaScript get automated checks?
questions.why: Both bugs you just had me fix were in `app.js`, and neither was reachable from the Python suite — I verified the fixes by driving headless Chrome. That check could be a committed script instead of something I did once by hand.

options.label: A committed script that drives headless Chrome
options.detail: No npm, no new runtime dependency — it uses a browser that is already on the machine, and skips cleanly when one isn't. Covers exactly the class of bug that got through.

options.label: A real JS test runner
options.detail: Better tooling and assertions. Cost: breaks the no-npm, no-build-step constraint, which is the reason the tool is expected to still run in a year.

options.label: Nothing automated — check by hand when the JS changes
options.detail: Zero added machinery. Cost: this is the status quo that shipped both bugs.

questions.prompt: Anything here worth building into v1?
questions.why: These are cheap individually and easy to skip. Picking none is a fine answer — I would rather ship the core clean than pad it.

options.label: `qsurface --version`
options.detail: Tells you which install you are actually running when two exist.

options.label: `qsurface doctor`
options.detail: Verifies the skill is linked, the CLI is on PATH, and the Python version is supported. Useful on a fresh machine.

options.label: `qsurface show --open`
options.detail: Opens the last response's markdown render in a browser for reading.

options.label: Follow-up questionnaires that carry the prior response as context
options.detail: For the 'repeat as needed' half of the loop — a second round that shows what was already decided.

options.label: `qsurface archive <id>`
options.detail: Moves a finished questionnaire out of the active list without deleting its responses.

questions.prompt: Anything I have not asked that would change the design?
questions.why: The questions above are the forks I can see from the code. You have the intent behind the tool, which I only have secondhand.
